en: His heart broke once more.
In the loudly neighing Bozaiman
He seemed to see his forefather Manas.
Neighing and whinnying,
The stallion lowered his head to the ground,
And circled around
Your honored Sary Khan.
When the stallion behaved this way—
We do not know the truth of it;
Much is false and much is true,
For no one who saw it has returned.
We made it a tale for diversion,
To recount the deeds
Of heroes long vanished.
Half is invention and half is truth;
No soul has come back from beyond—
Only the Creator Himself knows.
At that moment Bozaiman stood,
His tail and mane streaming apart.
He had no tongue with which to speak,
So the creature neighed,
And tears poured from his eyes.
When they settled in broad Talas
And livestock filled the valley,
Wise Sary Khan
Was out ranging with his herds.
Aimanboz, then an eight-year-old,
When dawn shone clear
And light touched the earth,
Appeared to him from the unseen.
When he reached eight years of age,
Sary Khan found him,
Tied a plume upon his head,
And kept him as a breeding stallion.
Mares covered by that stallion foaled,
And from Bozaiman himself
Came dark bay noble steeds,
With broad lungs and brazen legs,
Horses fit to ride into battle.
His tail was an armful, and full was his mane—
Such was the creature, if you measured him.
When they saw the gray stallion,
The birches wept and the willows wept,
Every living witness wept,
The earth shook and the grass wept,
And poor Külchoro wept without end.
His uncle Sary Khan,
His elder dearer than a father,
Had died while fighting,
Suffering death at the madman’s hands.
He grasped him at the waist and folded him,
Crying, “Do not die, my lionhearted uncle!”
Then he loaded him upon Bozaiman.
By the black springs of Kainar,
Beside the straight plane tree,
Below Tört-Kül,
In the garden planted by noble khans,
Facing Jylgynduu,
On the near side of Keng-Kol,
In the lower hollow of Keng-Shor,
Along Tal-Mazar,
He hacked and hollowed out
A grave-shaped place,
And hiding his face from sight,
He laid Sary Khan to rest.
Leaving none of his grief unspoken,
He tried to drive Bozaiman away.
Whinnying mournfully,
The gray stallion would not obey.
Though beaten, he balked and would not move;
The gray stallion refused.
Unable to turn his noble neck,
The gray stallion stood fast.
Like a wild ass, he turned his neck
Toward the qibla.
Though driven, he stood braying,
And the gray stallion would not move.
“Well then, if the ancient tales
Are true,
My creature, my gray stallion,
Go ahead to await my uncle Sary Khan.
Go as his companion, noble beast;
Go together with my uncle.
If you remain alive and ply the world,
No beast like you will ever leave mortal time.”
The mighty-born Külchoro
Seized both ears
Together with the forelock.
He made the stallion snort
And felled him where he stood.
Ah, that strong-born, mighty lion
Then cut off his head.
Until Sary Khan was buried,
Until the gray stallion was slaughtered—
Leave this matter here.
Now begin the tale of Kanchoro,
Whose soul departed amid matchlock fire
And the drawing of bows.
He gathered the Jediger and led the host,
So vast it made the earth sag.
The vanguard roared,
And when one looked upon the rising tumult,
They were shouting, “Kanchoro!”
He gathered the strong and led the host,
Leading no small force, but a multitude,
Driving the entire army together.
Firing matchlocks and drawing bows,
They surged forward
To surround the sultan upon the ridge,
And close around him,
To wage battle unto death,
To exact their vengeful grudge,
To bring a day of bitter grief,
And offer the gray-wolf hero Semetey
As a sacrifice.
The great dark host of Jediger,
Its ranks upon the rise roaring,
By the might of almighty God,
Charged to the last man.
The Jediger covered the earth,
Shouting “Kyyaz!” as their battle cry.
The army advanced and the people clamored,
Their renowned men at the front,
Their heroes along the flanks,
Ordered to seize and crush him,
While that fool Kanchoro stayed behind.
The host surged with a deafening uproar,
Striking the great war drum with a crash,
The trumpets deafening the ears,
The drums pounding loudly,
As they drew near the hero.
The clamorous army came onward.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
When he saw the onrushing host,
Felt his ribs torn apart;
Tears poured from his eyes,
And his heart was deeply troubled.
He tightened his belt in earnest,
And, unable to endure it,
His whole heart caught fire.
He gripped his spear and made ready,
And buckled on his scabbardless sword.
His sword would spare no life;
His heart was torn asunder.
Death’s grim, tumultuous work
Seemed very near
To the gray-wolf Choro’s eyes.
“Now my silver-eyed, sun-faced,
Thunder-voiced uncle,
The figure who gave me shelter,
My sovereign and sultan—
If the great dark Jediger horde
Overruns him while I give no aid,
What inheritance could satisfy me?
Before my uncle, towering like a rugged mountain,
I shall die first
And go as a sacrifice.
If I turn away in battle,
Though his shelter is worth a hundred armies,
And lose the one who shields me,
What inheritance could satisfy me?
He carved me meat and gave me fat,
And fed me butter when I hungered.
He sharpened and trained me for war.
Almambet, who departed for the other world,
Guarded me better than my father.
When I reached the age of six,
He had an amulet hung around my neck.
Wishing me to become a peerless gray wolf,
He raised me with tender affection,
Led me with him and made me a warrior,
And made me equal to his own heroic son.
He made me raid true Kakan and Beijing
Without the least mercy.
How could I let myself be parted
From my dark gray-wolf lion?
How could I abandon
My noble gray-wolf hero,
My fearsome, blood-spilling uncle?
The Jediger are ten thousand and I am alone,
Yet for seven months without rest
I shall fight them to mutual destruction.
Against the massed Jediger
I shall stand and level my spear;
For ninety days without rest I shall fight,
And unleash hellish wrath.
I shall rescue
My valiant lionhearted uncle;
I shall drive the strong before me and slaughter them.
For this peerless gray wolf
I shall fall as a sacrifice at his feet!”
Thus spoke Külchoro:
“I shall drive away their strongest.
Damn you, Jediger—
He who spares an enemy will be wounded;
He who spares his horse is left afield.
I shall strike down even the blameless
And make a slaughter of them.
I shall drive the boastful Jediger
Toward Jeti-Özön,
Make them cry, ‘Jakey, mercy!’
And force them truly to taste torment.
Those who survive the dead
I shall make cry, ‘Akebai, mercy!’
I shall make a glorious massacre.
Between Kyyaz and Kanchoro,
I shall take the head of one.
Before my uncle
I shall offer it in sacrifice.
While my uncle’s eyes still see,
I shall wage a battle,
Make their blood flow like water,
And exact my long-carried vengeance.
While his eyes are still alive,
For my lord, my gray-wolf uncle,
I shall become a sacrifice.
Making them cry, ‘Poor Choro!’
I shall unleash a mighty exchange of fire.”
Thus spoke Külchoro,
Thick-armed and stonehearted,
The broad-limbed, formidable warrior.
He buckled on his scabbardless sword;
The tiger-born lion Choro
Seemed about to become a storm,
Ready to slaughter whoever crossed his path.
Wrath spread across his face,
And he strained like a lion.
The formidable gray wolf
Found his battle cunning,
And thundered in anger.
No soul could withstand his awesome presence;
All men trembled.
He thundered in fury,
No soul able to withstand his might;
All who saw him quaked.
Behold what your Choro was like:
The bold and dashing lion Choro,
Peerless in swiftness,
The clashing hero Choro.
He looked to either side;
Behold your gray-wolf Choro,
Licking his lips.
Both champion and lion,
A hero poised like a falcon,
He made the whole world submit,
And threw all he faced into turmoil.
When he seized his sword with a shout,
Those who came against him
Were drenched in black blood.
Diviners judged and foretold
That he was the mightiest in the world.
When he swung his sword with a shout,
A great many
Of humankind perished.
Trembling at the sound of his name,
Even the people of distant Beijing withered.
